title: Display cultural awareness in dealing with clients and extensionists

lessons.title: Understanding culture in extension work
lessons.html:
Why culture matters to an extensionist

Culture is the shared set of values, beliefs, customs, language and ways of doing things that a group of people lives by. In South African extension work you will meet clients from many cultural backgrounds: isiZulu-speaking communal livestock owners in KwaZulu-Natal, Sesotho-speaking smallholders in the Free State, Afrikaans-speaking commercial grain farmers, Xhosa cattle owners in the Eastern Cape, and new entrants from land reform projects. Each group brings its own view of land, livestock, money, time, authority and change.

An extensionist who ignores culture often fails even when the technical advice is correct. A farmer may nod politely at a demonstration on reducing herd size, yet never act on it, because cattle in that community represent wealth, status, lobola and ancestral obligations rather than only a source of income. Advice that ignores this meaning will be rejected quietly.

Layers of culture

  • Visible culture: language, dress, food, ceremonies, greetings and farming methods you can observe directly.
  • Norms and roles: who speaks first in a meeting, the role of women and youth, how decisions are made in a household or traditional council.
  • Deep values: beliefs about land ownership, ancestors, risk, wealth and the relationship between people and nature.

Your own cultural lens

Every extensionist also carries a culture: training in scientific agriculture, a professional culture of government or a company, and a personal background. Cultural awareness starts with recognising your own assumptions. For example, you may assume that maximising yield per hectare is every farmer's goal, while a household may value food security, low risk and labour flexibility more.

Ask yourself before every field visit: What do I assume about this client? Where did that assumption come from? What would the client's view be? This self-reflection reduces stereotyping and helps you treat every client as an individual within a cultural context, not as a cultural label.

lessons.title: Communicating respectfully across cultures
lessons.html:
Practical cultural respect in the field

Respect is shown in small actions repeated consistently. In many rural communities, entry protocol is important. Before working in a communal area, first introduce yourself to the traditional leader (inkosi or induna) or the ward councillor, explain your purpose, and ask permission. Skipping this step can lead to a whole village avoiding your programme.

Greetings, language and time

  • Learn the correct greetings in the main local languages and use them. Even a few words show respect.
  • Use an interpreter from the community when you are not fluent, and brief the interpreter on technical terms beforehand.
  • Greet elders first and allow them to speak. Do not rush into business before the social greeting is complete.
  • Understand that views of time differ. Plan meetings around church days, funerals, pension pay-out days and the planting season.

Gender and age

In some households the man is the formal decision-maker even though women do most of the field work. Do not ignore women. Arrange separate sessions for women's groups or youth if mixed meetings prevent them from speaking. Address the household respectfully and include all those who carry out the work.

Dealing with fellow extensionists

Your colleagues also come from diverse backgrounds. Some were trained at agricultural colleges, others at universities; some have decades of field experience, others are new graduates. Respect different working styles, avoid jokes based on language or ethnicity, and resolve misunderstandings privately and early. Diverse teams are a strength because members can reach different communities.

What never to do

  • Never mock traditional practices, beliefs or remedies in front of clients.
  • Never make promises on behalf of the department or company that you cannot keep.
  • Never enter a homestead, kraal or field without being invited.

lessons.title: Working with traditional knowledge and resolving cultural conflict
lessons.html:
Building on what farmers already know

Indigenous knowledge is the knowledge farmers have built up over generations: reading the veld, timing planting by rain signs, selecting Nguni cattle for hardiness, mixing crops such as maize, beans and pumpkins. Much of it is sound and well adapted to local conditions. A culturally aware extensionist treats it as a starting point, not an obstacle.

When introducing new practice, link it to what is known. For example, explain that rotational grazing in camps builds on the old practice of moving herds to summer and winter grazing. Ask farmers to share their methods during demonstrations, and test new and old practices side by side in a farmer-managed trial.

When culture and advice clash

Sometimes a cultural practice creates a real risk, such as slaughtering a sick animal for a ceremony or sharing a dip tank without disease control. Handle such cases carefully:

  1. Listen first and understand why the practice exists and what it means.
  2. Explain the risk using local examples and plain language, not blame.
  3. Look for an option that respects the purpose of the practice while reducing the risk.
  4. Involve respected local leaders, elders or a local animal health technician.
  5. Where the law applies, for example controlled diseases under the Animal Diseases Act 35 of 1984, explain the legal duty clearly and refer to the state veterinarian.

Handling conflict between clients or colleagues

Cultural misunderstandings between groups, for example between a commercial farmer and neighbouring communal farmers over stray cattle, need a neutral facilitator. Keep to facts, give each side time to speak, and focus on shared interests such as safe roads, healthy herds and good neighbour relations.

Key points

  • Culture shapes how clients receive advice, so understand it before giving advice.
  • Recognise your own assumptions and avoid stereotypes.
  • Follow entry protocol and greet and involve elders, women and youth.
  • Use indigenous knowledge as a foundation for new practice.
  • Resolve cultural conflict by listening first and finding options that respect purpose and reduce risk.

quiz.question: Why might a farmer agree politely with advice to reduce herd size but never act on it?

options.text: Because cattle often carry social and cultural meaning beyond income
Because farmers do not understand any technical advice
Because herd size has no effect on veld condition
Because the extensionist spoke too slowly

quiz.question: What should you do before starting a programme in a communal area?

options.text: Start the demonstration immediately to save time
Introduce yourself to the traditional leader or councillor and ask permission
Visit each homestead unannounced
Send a written notice only to the youth

quiz.question: Which is an example of deep culture rather than visible culture?

options.text: Style of dress
Greetings used
Food eaten at ceremonies
Beliefs about land ownership and ancestors

quiz.question: Women in a community do not speak in mixed meetings. What is the best response?

options.text: Ignore women as the men make the decisions
Cancel the programme
Arrange separate sessions for women's groups
Insist that women speak first in every mixed meeting

quiz.question: What is the FIRST step when a cultural practice creates a real risk?

options.text: Report the farmer to the police
Tell the farmer the practice is backward
Ignore it to keep good relations
Listen and understand why the practice exists

quiz.question: Cultural awareness starts with recognising your own assumptions as an extensionist.

options.text: True
False

quiz.question: Indigenous knowledge should be replaced completely by scientific methods.

options.text: True
False

quiz.question: Which of these are things an extensionist should never do? (select all that apply)

options.text: Mock traditional practices in front of clients
Greet elders first
Make promises on behalf of the department that cannot be kept
Enter a kraal without being invited
Use a local interpreter
